gaps.subdomain: Alexander of Aphrodisias, Middle Platonists, Plotinus/Neoplatonists, Cicero, and the De Fato tradition
gaps.name: Origin-of-the-will controversy (Dihle vs. Frede vs. Bobzien)
gaps.why_canonical: The central modern-reception meta-debate for this whole subdomain: WHEN and WITH WHOM the concept of 'the will' / 'free will' emerged. Dihle 1982 (The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity) locates its invention in Augustine; M. Frede 2011 (A Free Will, Sather Lectures) argues it is a Stoic invention (Epictetus) and that Aristotle had no notion of will; Bobzien 1998b ('The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem', Phronesis 43) argues the genuine free-will PROBLEM appears only with Alexander of Aphrodisias. The KG has isolated nodes (concept_frede_general_schema, person Dihle implied, Bobzien) but no node tying them into the explicit three-way scholarly dispute that organizes the entire field.
gaps.source: Dihle 1982; M. Frede, A Free Will (2011); S. Bobzien, 'The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem', Phronesis 43 (1998) 133-175.

gaps.subdomain: Alexander of Aphrodisias, Middle Platonists, Plotinus/Neoplatonists, Cicero, and the De Fato tradition
gaps.name: The competing definitions of 'the possible' in Cicero De Fato (Diodorean vs. Philonian vs. Chrysippean)
gaps.why_canonical: Cicero De Fato 12-16 stages the core Hellenistic modal-determinism dispute: Diodorus Cronus' definition (only what is or will be true is possible), Philo the Dialectician's looser definition (capacity-based possibility), and Chrysippus' attempt to carve a middle position preserving contingency under causal determinism. This is THE locus classicus for the necessity/contingency axis of the fate debate. The KG has Diodorus, the Master Argument, and Bobzien's modal-logic shells, but no node for the three rival definitions of dynaton as such.
gaps.source: Cicero, De Fato 12-16; Bobzien, Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy (1998) ch. 3-4; Sharples, Cicero: On Fate (1991) commentary.

gaps.subdomain: Alexander of Aphrodisias, Middle Platonists, Plotinus/Neoplatonists, Cicero, and the De Fato tradition
gaps.name: Philo the Dialectician (Philo the Megarian / Philo of Megara)
gaps.why_canonical: The Megarian logician whose definition of 'the possible' is one of the two poles (against Diodorus) of the modal debate at Cicero De Fato 12-15 and a key input to Stoic modal theory. Diodorus Cronus already has a node (person_diodorus_cronus); his principal interlocutor Philo is absent, leaving the Master Argument / possibility dispute half-populated.
gaps.source: Cicero, De Fato 12-15; Bobzien, Determinism and Freedom (1998) ch. 3; Sedley, 'Diodorus Cronus and Hellenistic Philosophy', PCPS 23 (1977).

gaps.subdomain: Alexander of Aphrodisias, Middle Platonists, Plotinus/Neoplatonists, Cicero, and the De Fato tradition
gaps.name: Robert W. Sharples (R.W. Sharples)
gaps.why_canonical: The definitive modern editor, translator, and commentator of Alexander of Aphrodisias on fate: 'Alexander of Aphrodisias on Fate' (1983), the De Fato sections of the Mantissa and Quaestiones (Suppl. Arist.), and Cicero On Fate (1991). For the Alexander/De-Fato core of this subdomain he is at least as load-bearing as Bobzien (who already has a node). His six-position taxonomy of providence is even cited in the KG's existing scholarly_argument_sharples nodes, yet there is no person/scholar node for him.
gaps.source: R.W. Sharples, Alexander of Aphrodisias on Fate (Duckworth, 1983); Cicero: On Fate & Boethius: Consolation IV.5-7, V (Aris & Phillips, 1991).

gaps.subdomain: Alexander of Aphrodisias, Middle Platonists, Plotinus/Neoplatonists, Cicero, and the De Fato tradition
gaps.name: Alexander's open-alternatives / forking-paths argument against determinism (De Fato 11-15)
gaps.why_canonical: Alexander's signature positive case for to eph' hemin: deliberation and 'what is up to us' are intelligible only if more than one outcome is genuinely possible (the agent could have done otherwise), so causal determinism would abolish responsibility. This is the text Bobzien identifies as the birth of the genuine free-will problem and the locus of Alexander's contra-causal libertarianism. The KG has Alexander's Lazy-Argument and providence arguments and Zingano's liability-vs-possibility node, but not this central could-have-done-otherwise argument itself.
gaps.source: Alexander, De Fato 11-15 (Sharples 1983); Bobzien, Phronesis 43 (1998); Bobzien, 'Moral Responsibility and Moral Development in Epicurus and Alexander' (2014).

gaps.subdomain: Alexander of Aphrodisias, Middle Platonists, Plotinus/Neoplatonists, Cicero, and the De Fato tradition
gaps.name: Antiochus of Ascalon
gaps.why_canonical: The Academic who broke with skepticism and revived dogmatic Platonism, transmitting Stoic ethics/theology into the Platonist stream and shaping Cicero's philosophical sources (Academica, De Natura Deorum). He is the hinge between the New Academy (Carneades/Philo of Larissa, both present) and the Middle Platonist providence/fate doctrines (also present). His absence is a genealogical hole in the Academic-to-Platonist transmission for this subdomain.
gaps.source: Cicero, Academica I-II; J. Dillon, The Middle Platonists (1977/1996) ch. 2; Sedley (ed.), The Philosophy of Antiochus (2012).

gaps.subdomain: Alexander of Aphrodisias, Middle Platonists, Plotinus/Neoplatonists, Cicero, and the De Fato tradition
gaps.name: Freedom and self-causation of the One (Plotinus, Ennead VI.8)
gaps.why_canonical: Plotinus' radical extension of to eph' hemin and autexousion to the One/Good itself, describing it as self-determining and quasi-causa-sui (boulesis heautou) — the first metaphysics of absolute freedom and a turning point for Neoplatonic and later Christian conceptions of divine and human will. The KG has the work node (Ennead VI.8) and the Plotinian intellectual eph' hemin node, plus a Narbonne causa-sui scholarly shell, but no concept node for the freedom/self-causation of the One, which is the doctrinally distinctive contribution of VI.8.
gaps.source: Plotinus, Ennead VI.8 [39]; G. Leroux, Plotin: Traité sur la liberté et la volonté de l'Un (1990); K. Kalligas / J.-M. Narbonne on VI.8.

gaps.subdomain: Alexander of Aphrodisias, Middle Platonists, Plotinus/Neoplatonists, Cicero, and the De Fato tradition
gaps.name: Frede's 'two notions of necessity / two-strands' analysis of Stoic determinism (or: the eph' hemin vs. liberum-arbitrium conceptual shift)
gaps.why_canonical: The pivotal historiographical claim that ancient discussions operate with a notion of 'what is up to us' grounded in unimpeded rational agency, conceptually distinct from the later (Augustinian/medieval) notion of a free WILL choosing between alternatives — the very distinction that makes 'compatibilism/libertarian' labels anachronistic. The KG flags these labels as anachronistic (Phase 12) and has a terminology-evolution node, but lacks an explicit concept node articulating the eph'-hemin vs. liberum-arbitrium paradigm shift that underlies that whole policy.
gaps.source: M. Frede, A Free Will (2011); S. Bobzien, Determinism and Freedom (1998) Introduction; T. Brennan, The Stoic Life (2005).

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: Ammonius Hermeiou (Ammonius son of Hermeias, c. 435/445-517/526)
gaps.why_canonical: The Alexandrian Neoplatonist whose Greek commentary on Aristotle's De Interpretatione 9 is the single most important late-antique treatment of future contingents and divine foreknowledge between Aristotle and Boethius. Ammonius develops the 'definitely/indefinitely true-or-false' framework and the doctrine that God knows contingents 'in a determinate manner' without making them necessary — the exact apparatus Boethius deploys. Sorabji/Kretzmann/Mignucci 1998 (Ammonius/Boethius, On Aristotle On Interpretation 9) treat the two together as the joint hinge of the tradition. The KG has Boethius's De Int. commentary and the sea-battle node but is missing Ammonius entirely, leaving a hole at the very center of the foreknowledge/contingency thread.
gaps.source: R. Sorabji, N. Kretzmann, M. Mignucci, in D. Blank (trans.), Ammonius: On Aristotle On Interpretation 9 (Duckworth/Cornell, 1998); SEP 'Medieval Theories of Future Contingents'

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: Diodorus Cronus's Master Argument (ho kyrieuon logos / κυριεύων λόγος)
gaps.why_canonical: The foundational ancient argument linking modality, time and necessity: from (1) every past truth is necessary and (2) the impossible does not follow from the possible, Diodorus inferred that only what is or will be is possible — collapsing contingency into necessity. It is the direct ancestor of the De Interpretatione 9 problem, of Chrysippus's and the Stoics' modal responses, and of the whole foreknowledge/future-contingents tradition that runs through Ammonius and Boethius. Diodorus Cronus exists as a person node but his defining argument has no dedicated argument/concept node; Bobzien treats it as the central Hellenistic modal-fatalism argument.
gaps.source: S. Bobzien, Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy (OUP 1998), ch. 3; J. Vuillemin, Necessity or Contingency: The Master Argument (CSLI 1996)

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: Proclus's De Decem Dubitationes solution: divine foreknowledge is determinate cognition of indeterminate things (Ten Doubts Concerning Providence)
gaps.why_canonical: Proclus's De Decem Dubitationibus circa Providentiam (preserved in Moerbeke's Latin, one of the Tria Opuscula) gives the decisive Neoplatonic axiom that knowledge is according to the nature of the knower, not the known — so the gods know contingents determinately/timelessly without necessitating them. This is the proximate model for Boethius's Consolation V (modes-of-cognition argument) and a self-standing solution to the foreknowledge problem. The KG has the Tria Opuscula work node and a generic 'hierarchical providence' argument but not this specific, historically pivotal foreknowledge-solution argument.
gaps.source: C. Steel, Proclus: On Providence (Bloomsbury/Duckworth 2007); SEP 'Medieval Theories of Future Contingents'; Sorabji, Time, Creation and the Continuum

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: Nemesius's hierarchy/refutation argument: providence governs universals, to eph' hemin governs particulars (De Natura Hominis 42-43)
gaps.why_canonical: Nemesius's positive constructive account — distinguishing what falls under providence from what is 'up to us', and surveying/refuting six views on the scope of providence and fate — is his core contribution to the fate debate and a key source for John of Damascus and Byzantine theology. The KG has several Amand-1945-sourced Nemesius astrology-refutation arguments (Nat. Hom. 35-38) but lacks his systematic providence-vs-eph'hemin doxography and the De Fato section, which Sharples/Telfer treat as the most sophisticated late-antique synthesis.
gaps.source: R.W. Sharples & P.J. van der Eijk (trans.), Nemesius: On the Nature of Man (Liverpool UP 2008); W. Telfer, Cyril of Jerusalem and Nemesius of Emesa (LCC 1955)

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: Richard Sorabji (modern reception scholar)
gaps.why_canonical: Sorabji is the central modern authority on late-antique time, eternity, necessity and the future-contingents tradition (Time, Creation and the Continuum 1983; Necessity, Cause and Blame 1980; editor of the Ancient Commentators on Aristotle series including the Ammonius/Boethius volume). For a KG covering Boethius/Proclus/Nemesius/foreknowledge, his absence as a modern-reception node is conspicuous — Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji form the standard trio and only Sorabji-the-person needs anchoring of his foreknowledge/eternity work specifically.
gaps.source: R. Sorabji, Necessity, Cause and Blame (Duckworth 1980); Time, Creation and the Continuum (Duckworth 1983)

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: John Marenbon (modern reception scholar on Boethius)
gaps.why_canonical: Marenbon (Boethius, OUP 2003) is the leading contemporary anglophone interpreter of Boethius's foreknowledge/eternity argument, the simple-vs-conditional-necessity distinction, and the 'relational' reading of divine cognition. The KG has the Boethian arguments and concepts (duplex necessitas, nunc stans, aeternitas) but no modern-reception node tying them to the dominant modern interpreter, leaving the secondary-layer thin precisely where the primary layer is strong.
gaps.source: J. Marenbon, Boethius (Oxford University Press, 2003)

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: Robert W. Sharples (modern reception scholar on fate/providence)
gaps.why_canonical: Sharples is the standard editor/interpreter of Alexander of Aphrodisias's De Fato, of Cicero's De Fato, and of Nemesius, and authored the canonical taxonomy of six positions [A]-[F] on the scope of providence that the KG already cites in scholarly_argument nodes. Yet there is no Sharples person node to anchor those scholarly arguments — a structural gap given how often the existing graph leans on his work for the fate/providence sub-domain.
gaps.source: R.W. Sharples, Cicero: On Fate & Boethius: Consolation IV.5-7, V (Aris & Phillips 1991); Alexander of Aphrodisias on Fate (Duckworth 1983)

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: Conditional/relational reading of divine foreknowledge (knowledge follows the mode of the knower, not the known)
gaps.why_canonical: The general epistemological principle — modus cognoscendi follows the nature of the cognizing subject — is the shared engine of the Proclean and Boethian solutions to the foreknowledge problem (Boethius, Consolation V.pr.4-6; Proclus, De Decem Dub.). The KG has nunc stans, aeternitas and the Boethian 'modes of cognition' argument, but not this cross-cutting concept as its own node, which would link Ammonius, Proclus, Boethius and the later medieval debate that the KG already represents.
gaps.source: J. Marenbon, Boethius (OUP 2003), ch. on prescience; C. Steel, Proclus: On Providence (2007)

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: The standard/Stoic vs. anti-realist (third-truth-value) interpretation of De Interpretatione 9
gaps.why_canonical: Whether Aristotle in De Int. 9 abandons bivalence for future contingents (the Ammonius-Boethius 'indefinitely true/false' reading) or retains it (the modern 'standard' reading) is the defining modern scholarly debate on the text, prosecuted by Anscombe, Hintikka, Frede, Mignucci, Gaskin and Sorabji. The KG has the sea-battle and Boethius-future-contingents argument nodes but no debate node capturing this interpretive controversy that organizes the entire secondary literature on the foreknowledge/contingency problem.
gaps.source: R. Gaskin, The Sea Battle and the Master Argument (de Gruyter 1995); D. Frede, 'The Sea-Battle Reconsidered', OSAP 3 (1985); SEP 'Future Contingents'

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: Ammonius, In Aristotelis De Interpretatione Commentarius (on De Int. 9)
gaps.why_canonical: The primary text underlying the entire late-antique foreknowledge/future-contingents discussion and the proximate Greek background to Boethius's two commentaries (which the KG already has). Edited Busse, CAG IV.5; translated Blank 1998. Without this work node the KG's De Int. 9 cluster jumps from Aristotle straight to Boethius, omitting the crucial Alexandrian intermediary.
gaps.source: A. Busse (ed.), Ammonius In De Interpretatione, CAG IV.5 (Berlin 1897); D. Blank (trans.), Ammonius On Aristotle On Interpretation 9 (1998)

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: Proclus, De Decem Dubitationibus circa Providentiam (Ten Doubts Concerning Providence)
gaps.why_canonical: One of the three Tria Opuscula (the KG has only the umbrella Tria Opuscula node and a separate De Providentia node), De Decem Dub. is the specific treatise where Proclus solves the foreknowledge-vs-contingency problem via the knower-relative cognition principle. It deserves its own work node as the direct source for Boethius's Consolation V and a named primary text in the foreknowledge thread.
gaps.source: C. Steel (ed./trans.), Proclus: Ten Problems Concerning Providence / On Providence (Bloomsbury 2007); Boese (ed.), Procli Tria Opuscula (1960)

gaps.subdomain: Boethius, Proclus, Nemesius, foreknowledge/eternity, late-antique fate debates
gaps.name: Calcidius's treatment of fate and providence (Commentary on the Timaeus, ch. 142-190)
gaps.why_canonical: Calcidius's long Latin excursus on fatum/providentia/possibile (drawing on Middle Platonist and Peripatetic sources, partly via a lost source shared with Pseudo-Plutarch) is the principal Latin transmission of the conditional-fate doctrine to the Latin West before Boethius, and a key witness in the Amand/Den Boeft scholarship the KG already engages. Calcidius exists as a thin person node (160 chars, no work/argument) — his fate-providence treatise is absent.
gaps.source: J. den Boeft, Calcidius on Fate (Brill 1970); G. Boys-Stones, Platonist Philosophy 80 BC to AD 250 (CUP 2018)

gaps.subdomain: Presocratics + Plato + Aristotle on voluntary action, eph' hemin, prohairesis, the sea-battle
gaps.name: Gorgias of Leontini
gaps.source: Gorgias, Encomium of Helen (DK 82 B11); R. Barney, 'Gorgias: Encomium of Helen' (commentary); SEP 'Ancient Theories of Freedom and Determinism' notes the Homeric/tragic compatibilist backdrop Gorgias exploits
gaps.why_canonical: Wholly absent (no person, work, or argument node). The Encomium of Helen is the earliest extant systematic analysis of excusing conditions: Gorgias argues that divine necessity/fate, physical force, persuasive logos, and erōs are each forms of compulsion that void voluntary action and hence responsibility. This is the proto-text of the 'compulsion vs. voluntary' framework that Aristotle later formalizes in EN III.1, and a key sophistic data point in the prehistory of eph' hemin and moral responsibility.

gaps.subdomain: Presocratics + Plato + Aristotle on voluntary action, eph' hemin, prohairesis, the sea-battle
gaps.name: Socratic denial of akrasia / 'no one does wrong willingly' (Protagoras 352-358, Meno, Gorgias 468)
gaps.source: Plato, Protagoras 358b-d (οὐδεὶς ἑκὼν ἁμαρτάνει); H. Segvic, 'No One Errs Willingly: The Meaning of Socratic Intellectualism' (OSAP 19, 2000); T. Irwin, Plato's Ethics
gaps.why_canonical: Socratic Intellectualism exists only as a static concept node; the actual argument — that wrongdoing is always involuntary because it stems from ignorance, so virtue is knowledge and akrasia is impossible — is not modeled as an ancient argument node. It is the single most-cited Platonic locus for the claim that the early Greek tradition had no notion of a will independent of reason (the 'intellectualism thesis' of Dihle/Frede that the KG already tracks on the reception side), so the primary-source argument it answers to is a structural gap.

gaps.subdomain: Presocratics + Plato + Aristotle on voluntary action, eph' hemin, prohairesis, the sea-battle
gaps.name: Aristotle's conditions of (in)voluntariness: force (bia) and ignorance (EN III.1, 1109b30-1111b3)
gaps.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.1; Eudemian Ethics II.6-9; S. Meyer, Aristotle on Moral Responsibility; SEP 'Ancient Theories of Freedom and Determinism'
gaps.why_canonical: The KG has hekousion/akousion concept nodes and a 'voluntary action argument', but the foundational analytic argument of EN III.1 — that an act is involuntary iff its origin (archē) is external (force) or it is done in ignorance of particulars, with mixed/coerced actions and the 'pain + regret' criterion — is present only through modern scholarly glosses (Labarrière, Meyer, Echeñique). This passage is the historical seedbed of the entire eph' hemin tradition and deserves a first-class ancient argument node, distinct from the prohairesis analysis.

gaps.subdomain: Presocratics + Plato + Aristotle on voluntary action, eph' hemin, prohairesis, the sea-battle
gaps.name: Aristotle on responsibility for character: 'we are co-causes (sunaitioi) of our states' (EN III.5, 1113b3-1114b25)
gaps.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.5 1114a31-b25; S. Bobzien, 'Found in Translation: Aristotle's nicomachean ethics 3.5 1113b7-8 and its reception' (OSAP 2014); S. Meyer, Aristotle on Moral Responsibility
gaps.why_canonical: Only a thin Bobzien-2014 reception gloss (anti-indeterminist reading of 1113b7-8) and a Meyer scholarly-argument exist; the underlying ancient argument — that since we voluntarily acquire our dispositions through habituation, we are responsible (sunaitioi) for our characters and hence for the ends they make appear good — is not modeled. This is the locus classicus debated by every reader who asks whether Aristotle has a 'could-have-done-otherwise' notion, and the central battleground (Furley, Sorabji, Bobzien) over whether EN III is libertarian or compatibilist.

gaps.subdomain: Presocratics + Plato + Aristotle on voluntary action, eph' hemin, prohairesis, the sea-battle
gaps.name: Standard vs. traditional interpretation of De Interpretatione 9 (restriction of bivalence for future contingents)
gaps.source: Aristotle, De Int. 9 19a23-39; D. Frede, 'The Sea-Battle Reconsidered' (OSAP 1985); J. Hintikka, Time and Necessity (1973); R. Sorabji, Necessity, Cause and Blame (1980); G. Fine; Weidemann ed.
gaps.why_canonical: The sea-battle argument node and concept node exist, but the central scholarly DEBATE over it is unmodeled: does Aristotle reject bivalence (Frede, Lukasiewicz, Crivelli 'standard' view) or only the necessity inference while keeping bivalence (Anscombe, Hintikka, 'non-standard')? This interpretive fork is the most-discussed question in the whole logical-fatalism strand and the hinge for whether Aristotle answers the fatalist argument at all. Should be a debate node linking De Int. 9 to the Stoic bivalence-acceptance argument already present.

gaps.subdomain: Presocratics + Plato + Aristotle on voluntary action, eph' hemin, prohairesis, the sea-battle
gaps.name: Plato's self-moving soul as archē kinēseōs (Phaedrus 245c-246a; Laws X 894b-896b)
gaps.source: Plato, Phaedrus 245c-e; Laws X 895e-896b; S. Menn / J. Campbell, 'Self-Motion and Cognition: Plato's Theory of the Soul' (SJP 2021); R. Marinescu, 'Plato on Self-Motion in Laws X'
gaps.why_canonical: The Laws X self-motion argument node exists but is a 208-char stub and the Phaedrus parallel is absent. Plato's claim that soul is the self-mover and source/origin (pēgē kai archē) of all motion is the principal Platonic resource for grounding agent-origination and a recognized antecedent of Aristotle's 'origin in the agent' criterion and of later autexousion theology. Worth enriching to first-class status and linking to eph' hemin and agent-causation.

gaps.subdomain: Presocratics + Plato + Aristotle on voluntary action, eph' hemin, prohairesis, the sea-battle
gaps.name: The 'late and inadvertent birth' of the free-will problem (Bobzien's developmental thesis: Aristotle to Alexander)
gaps.source: S. Bobzien, 'The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem' (Phronesis 43, 1998) and Determinism, Freedom, and Moral Responsibility (OUP 2021); SEP 'Ancient Theories of Freedom and Determinism'
gaps.why_canonical: There is a one-line scholarly-argument stub (bobzien_origin_of_the_free_will_proble_0) but no proper concept/debate node for the single most influential periodization thesis in the field: that classical and Hellenistic thinkers debated eph' hemin without any notion of freedom-to-do-otherwise, and the free-will problem proper only crystallizes with Alexander. It is the organizing framework against which the entire Presocratic-to-Aristotle subdomain should be read, and structures the KG's own period assignments.

gaps.subdomain: Presocratics + Plato + Aristotle on voluntary action, eph' hemin, prohairesis, the sea-battle
gaps.name: Determinism in early atomism: Democritus/Leucippus 'nothing happens at random' (DK 68 B118/A66) vs. attribution of chance
gaps.source: Leucippus DK 67 B2; Aristotle Physics II.4 196a24-35; D. Sedley, 'Epicurean Anti-Reductionism'; M. R. Johnson 2014 on Democritus; SEP entry on Democritus
gaps.why_canonical: Democritus, Leucippus, and 'Democritean atomistic determinism' exist as nodes, but the genuine ancient/scholarly debate — whether the atomists were strict necessitarians (Aristotle's complaint that they reduced all to necessity and 'banished chance') or left room for tuchē/spontaneity, and how Epicurus' swerve responds — is not modeled as a debate node. This is the origin point of cosmological determinism that the whole downstream eph' hemin tradition reacts against, and the KG already has the Epicurus/swerve side but not the framing dispute.

gaps.subdomain: Presocratics + Plato + Aristotle on voluntary action, eph' hemin, prohairesis, the sea-battle
gaps.name: Aristotle: deliberation/choice presuppose the contingent and 'what is up to us' (EN III.3 1112a18-1113a14)
gaps.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.3 1112a18-1113a14; M. Crubellier and C. Natali on Aristotelian deliberation; Sorabji, Necessity Cause and Blame ch. 14
gaps.why_canonical: The prohairesis analysis node covers choice, but Aristotle's specific argument that we deliberate only about things that are up to us and capable of being otherwise (not the eternal, the necessary, or the impossible) — directly tying eph' hemin to contingency — is captured only in scattered scholarly glosses. It is the explicit Aristotelian link between the modal notion of contingency and the practical notion of agency, and the bridge between the De Int. 9 contingency strand and the ethics strand.

gaps.subdomain: Greek + Latin Fathers on autexousion/liberum arbitrium: Justin, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Maximus, anti-astrology/anti-fatalism
gaps.name: John of Damascus, Expositio fidei (De fide orthodoxa) II.12 + II.22-30 (chapters on the image of God / autexousion, on what is and is not 'up to us' [τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν], on providence, foreknowledge and predestination, and on free choice [περὶ αὐτεξουσίου])
gaps.why_canonical: Person node person_john_damascene_d749 exists as a thin 264-char shell with ZERO works and ZERO arguments, yet John's Expositio fidei is the great late-patristic systematization of the entire Greek free-will tradition (Nemesius, Maximus, the Cappadocians): it codifies autexousion as a corollary of the rational soul/image of God, the distinction of φύσει vs. προαιρετικῶς, the natural vs. gnomic will inherited from Maximus, and the careful sorting of what falls under providence vs. 'what is up to us'. It is the textbook through which this doctrine passed to Byzantium and (via Burgundio's Latin) to the scholastics. Its near-total absence is the single largest person-level gap in this sub-domain.
gaps.source: documentacatholicaomnia.eu critical text of De Fide Orthodoxa Bk II (chs. on αὐτεξούσιον / providence / foreknowledge); A. Kimel, 'Maximus the Confessor and John of Damascus on Gnomic Will (γνώμη) in Christ' (cites De fide orth. III.14, 18 and II on autexousion)

gaps.subdomain: Greek + Latin Fathers on autexousion/liberum arbitrium: Justin, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Maximus, anti-astrology/anti-fatalism
gaps.name: Origen's pre-existence of rational souls (λογικά) and pre-cosmic fall as free-will theodicy (De Principiis II.9)
gaps.why_canonical: Origen is extremely well covered for his anti-astrology and prescience≠cause arguments, but the metaphysical engine of his free-will theodicy is absent as a discrete concept: the equal creation of rational beings and their differential FALL through free choice, which explains the diversity of cosmic stations (angels/humans/demons) WITHOUT impugning divine justice and WITHOUT Gnostic natures. Scholarship (Martens, Scott 'Journey Back to God', Ramelli) treats this as the foundational move that lets Origen reconcile a just creator with manifest inequality precisely by grounding it in autexousion rather than fate or nature. It is the doctrinal core later condemned in 553 and the reason the Origenist free-will model is distinctive.
gaps.source: M. S. M. Scott, Journey Back to God: Origen on the Problem of Evil (OUP 2012); P. Martens, 'Origen's Doctrine of Pre-Existence and the Opening Chapters of Genesis', ZAC 16 (2013) 516-549; Origen De Principiis II.9

gaps.subdomain: Greek + Latin Fathers on autexousion/liberum arbitrium: Justin, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Maximus, anti-astrology/anti-fatalism
gaps.name: Gregory of Nyssa's double creation and 'garments of skin' (δερμάτινοι χιτῶνες) as free-will anthropology (De hominis opificio 16-17; De anima et resurrectione)
gaps.why_canonical: Gregory's anti-fatalism (Contra Fatum) and his image-of-God argument for autexousion are present, but the protological-soteriological framework that grounds them — the distinction between the first (timeless, sexless, in-the-image) creation and the second (embodied, mortal) creation, with the 'garments of skin' as the consequence of the free turn away from the good — is missing. This is precisely the structure that lets Gregory locate evil in the misuse of προαίρεσις (a privation, παρυπόστασις) and frame mortality/embodiment as remedial rather than punitive, undergirding apokatastasis as the eventual restoration of all free wills. Standard in Nyssen scholarship (Daniélou, Ludlow, Boersma).
gaps.source: J. Daniélou, L'être et le temps chez Grégoire de Nysse (1970); M. Ludlow, Universal Salvation: Eschatology in the Thought of Gregory of Nyssa and Karl Rahner (OUP 2000); Gregory, De hominis opificio 16-17

gaps.subdomain: Greek + Latin Fathers on autexousion/liberum arbitrium: Justin, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Maximus, anti-astrology/anti-fatalism
gaps.name: Augustine, Ad Simplicianum de diuersis quaestionibus I.2 (396 CE)
gaps.why_canonical: Augustine's De libero arbitrio, De gratia et libero arbitrio, De correptione, De praedestinatione, De dono perseuerantiae and Confessiones VIII are all present, but Ad Simplicianum — the work Augustine himself (Retract. II.1; De dono pers. 20-21) identifies as the hinge where he concluded that even the initial movement of faith is God's gift and that election precedes merit (vocatio congrua, the exegesis of Romans 9) — is absent. It is treated across the literature (Wetzel, TeSelle, Carol Harrison's continuity thesis) as THE turning point in the free-will/grace question, more pivotal than any single later anti-Pelagian treatise. Its omission leaves a documented gap in the causal chain of Augustine's volte-face.
gaps.source: J. Wetzel, Augustine and the Limits of Virtue (1992) on Ad Simpl. as 'a veritable revolution'; C. Harrison, Rethinking Augustine's Early Theology (OUP 2006); Augustine, Retractationes II.1

gaps.subdomain: Greek + Latin Fathers on autexousion/liberum arbitrium: Justin, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Maximus, anti-astrology/anti-fatalism
gaps.name: John Chrysostom on synergy, autexousion and the limits of grace (Homiliae in Romanos, esp. Hom. 16 on Rom 9; De fato et providentia / Ad Stagirium; Quod nemo laeditur nisi a se ipso)
gaps.why_canonical: person_john_chrysostom_d407 has a substantial description but NO work nodes and NO argument nodes in this sub-domain. Chrysostom is the principal Antiochene voice asserting robust autexousion and a 'first move from us, then grace' synergism (τὸ πᾶν / τὸ πλέον debate), and his anti-fatalist treatise Ad Stagirium and the homilies on Romans 9 are a standard counterweight to the Augustinian reading of Paul in the Greek tradition. His absence at the work/argument level is a real lacuna given that the KG already models Diodore of Tarsus, Theodoret and the Antiochene anti-fatalist line.
gaps.source: R. A. Layton & A. Bathrellou on Greek synergism; M. Lamberigts, 'Predestination' entries on the Greek (Antiochene) alternative to Augustine; Chrysostom, In ep. ad Romanos hom. 16 (PG 60)

gaps.subdomain: Greek + Latin Fathers on autexousion/liberum arbitrium: Justin, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Maximus, anti-astrology/anti-fatalism
gaps.name: Privation theory of evil (στέρησις / privatio boni) as condition of free-will theodicy (Plotinus → Basil → Gregory of Nyssa → Augustine → Pseudo-Dionysius)
gaps.why_canonical: The KG has Christian theodicy, Methodian 'evil as accident not substance', and origin-of-evil material, but not the unifying privation-of-the-good doctrine as a NAMED cross-author concept. This is the metaphysical premise that makes the free-will defence work for nearly every Father in scope: if evil has no substantial cause, then its only 'cause' is the deficient/free turning of the rational will, so God is exonerated. It is the explicit bridge between the Neoplatonic and the patristic free-will theodicies and is treated as such throughout the secondary literature.
gaps.source: Augustine, Confessiones VII & De natura boni; J. Rist, 'Plotinus on Matter and Evil'; standard treatments in Bobzien/Sorabji and in the Stanford Encyclopedia entries on the problem of evil in late antiquity

gaps.subdomain: Greek + Latin Fathers on autexousion/liberum arbitrium: Justin, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Maximus, anti-astrology/anti-fatalism
gaps.name: Maximus the Confessor: γνώμη/gnomic deliberation as a post-lapsarian deficiency abolished in the eschaton (not constitutive of the imago) — and its absence in Christ
gaps.why_canonical: The KG has good Maximus coverage (natural vs gnomic will, dyothelitism, two energies, baptismal repair, Blowers scholarly arguments). The one underdeveloped node would be the explicit ARGUMENT that gnomic will is itself a defect of fallen mutability rather than a perfection of freedom — the reason Christ has a natural human will but NO gnomic will, and the reason the saints lose γνώμη in deification. This is the conceptual payoff that distinguishes Maximus's account of freedom from a leeway/choice account and is the crux of the dyothelite settlement; worth isolating from the existing 'natural vs gnomic' descriptive node.
gaps.source: P. M. Blowers, Maximus the Confessor: Jesus Christ and the Transfiguration of the World (OUP 2016); I. McFarland, 'Naturally and by Grace: Maximus the Confessor on the Operation of the Will', SJT 58 (2005)

gaps.subdomain: Greek + Latin Fathers on autexousion/liberum arbitrium: Justin, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Maximus, anti-astrology/anti-fatalism
gaps.name: Bardaisan / 'Book of the Laws of Countries' (Liber legum regionum, the dialogue of Philip recording Bardaisan)
gaps.why_canonical: person_bardesanes_the_syrian exists with a rich description, but the actual source — the Book of the Laws of Countries — has no work node. It is the single most important Syriac contribution to the anti-astrology / free-will debate: it deploys the 'laws of countries' (nomima barbarika) argument empirically against astral determinism while distinguishing nature, fate and freedom (kyānā / heḏrā / ḥērūṯā). Given that the KG already models the nomima barbarika argument extensively (Amand 1945 line) and credits Carneades, the originating Syriac text deserves its own work node.
gaps.source: H. J. W. Drijvers, Bardaiṣan of Edessa (1966); ed./trans. of the Liber Legum Regionum; cited in Amand de Mendieta, Fatalisme et liberté dans l'antiquité grecque (1945)

gaps.subdomain: Modern scholars of ancient free will (Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji, Sharples, Dihle, Long, Salles, Destrée, Fürst)
gaps.name: Richard Sorabji, Necessity, Cause and Blame: Perspectives on Aristotle's Theory (Duckworth, 1980)
gaps.why_canonical: Sorabji is a named target scholar present as a person node, but his single most important monograph on determinism/free will is absent (only his Emotion and Peace of Mind is present). It is the standard treatment of Aristotle on necessity, cause, voluntariness and culpability; its thesis that Aristotle separates necessity from causation (rejecting both universal determinism and the inference that an uncaused event is uncausable) is foundational to all subsequent work on ancient incompatibilism and is cited throughout Bobzien, Frede and Sharples.
gaps.source: R. Sorabji, Necessity, Cause and Blame (Duckworth/Cornell 1980); praised by Nussbaum; PhilPapers SORNCA

gaps.subdomain: Modern scholars of ancient free will (Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji, Sharples, Dihle, Long, Salles, Destrée, Fürst)
gaps.name: A.A. Long & D.N. Sedley, The Hellenistic Philosophers (Cambridge, 1987), esp. sections 20 (Causation), 38 (Determinism), 62 (Free will and determinism)
gaps.why_canonical: A.A. Long is a named target scholar present as a person node, but the standard sourcebook of the field is absent. Its thematically organized sections on causation, determinism and eph' hemin are the canonical citation backbone for the entire Hellenistic free-will literature; the KG's Stoic/Epicurean fate nodes implicitly depend on it.
gaps.source: A.A. Long & D.N. Sedley, The Hellenistic Philosophers, 2 vols (CUP 1987); JHS review; PhilPapers LONTHP-5/6

gaps.subdomain: Modern scholars of ancient free will (Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji, Sharples, Dihle, Long, Salles, Destrée, Fürst)
gaps.name: Susanne Bobzien, Determinism, Freedom, and Moral Responsibility: Essays in Ancient Philosophy (Oxford, 2021)
gaps.why_canonical: Bobzien is the central named scholar; her 1998 monograph is present but her 2021 collected-essays volume — gathering her field-defining articles (incl. on Epicurus, the inadvertent conception of the free-will problem, Chrysippean compatibilism, the two-sided 'in our power') — is absent. It is the consolidated statement of the most influential living position on ancient free will and now the standard citation for her anachronism thesis.
gaps.source: S. Bobzien, Determinism, Freedom, and Moral Responsibility (OUP 2021), ISBN 9780198866732; PhilPapers BOBDFA-2

gaps.subdomain: Modern scholars of ancient free will (Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji, Sharples, Dihle, Long, Salles, Destrée, Fürst)
gaps.name: Susanne Bobzien, 'Did Epicurus Discover the Free Will Problem?', Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy 19 (2000), 287-337
gaps.why_canonical: The single most-cited modern intervention denying that Epicurus founded the free-will debate. The KG already has argument nodes paraphrasing the thesis but lacks the bibliographic work node itself, leaving those claims un-anchored to their source; it governs interpretation of the KG's Epicurus/clinamen and 'Epicurus and Free Will Problem' debate nodes.
gaps.source: S. Bobzien, OSAP 19 (2000): 287-337; PhilArchive BOBDED; reprinted in her 2021 essays

gaps.subdomain: Modern scholars of ancient free will (Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji, Sharples, Dihle, Long, Salles, Destrée, Fürst)
gaps.name: DATA FIX: person_frede_michael_1940_2007 mislabeled 'Dorothea Frede' (66-char stub), duplicating scholar_frede_michael and scholar_frede_dorothea
gaps.why_canonical: Michael Frede (1940-2007), author of the Sather Lectures A Free Will (2011, already a work node), is a named target scholar. The person node keyed to his ID and dates carries the wrong label ('Dorothea Frede') and is a near-empty stub, while two parallel scholar_* nodes also exist. This node-identity/dedup error fragments the most important reception-side authorship in the subdomain; the canonical Michael Frede should be one well-described node linked to work_frede_free_will_2011.
gaps.source: M. Frede, A Free Will, ed. A.A. Long (UC Press 2011), Sather Classical Lectures 68

gaps.subdomain: Modern scholars of ancient free will (Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji, Sharples, Dihle, Long, Salles, Destrée, Fürst)
gaps.name: R.W. Sharples, Alexander of Aphrodisias: On Fate (Duckworth, 1983) and Cicero: On Fate / Boethius (Aris & Phillips, 1991)
gaps.why_canonical: Sharples is a named target scholar present as a person node, but the editions that made him indispensable — his text/translation/commentary of Alexander De Fato and Cicero De Fato — are absent even though the KG has work_de_fato_alexander and work_de_fato_cicero. These are the standard English critical editions cited for both anti-Stoic fate treatises; without them the corpus' two central fate texts lack their canonical modern apparatus.
gaps.source: R.W. Sharples, Alexander of Aphrodisias: On Fate (Duckworth 1983); Cicero: On Fate / Boethius (Aris & Phillips 1991)

gaps.subdomain: Modern scholars of ancient free will (Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji, Sharples, Dihle, Long, Salles, Destrée, Fürst)
gaps.name: Michael Frede, 'The Original Notion of Cause', in Doubt and Dogmatism (eds. Schofield/Burnyeat/Barnes, Oxford 1980), 217-249
gaps.why_canonical: Frede's classic paper reconstructing the Stoic theory of causes (perfect/principal vs auxiliary causes) is the standard reference for the causal taxonomy underlying Chrysippean compatibilism and the cylinder analogy — both present as KG nodes but lacking this anchoring secondary source. One of the most cited articles on ancient causation.
gaps.source: M. Frede, 'The Original Notion of Cause', in Doubt and Dogmatism, eds. Schofield/Burnyeat/Barnes (Clarendon 1980), 217-249

gaps.subdomain: Modern scholars of ancient free will (Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji, Sharples, Dihle, Long, Salles, Destrée, Fürst)
gaps.name: Alfons Fürst, Wege zur Freiheit (Mohr Siebeck, 2022) and the Münster Origenes critical-edition / Origenes Handbuch project
gaps.why_canonical: Fürst is a named target scholar and the leading modern interpreter of Origen's Freiheitsmetaphysik; the KG already has concept nodes citing 'Fürst 2022' and 'Hengstermann 2016' but the monograph those nodes paraphrase, and the Münster edition project that defines current Origen-on-free-will scholarship, are not present as work/reference nodes, leaving the German reception strand un-sourced. Confirmed present in the local library.
gaps.source: A. Fürst, Wege zur Freiheit (Mohr Siebeck 2022); local 04_Littérature_secondaire/05_Origene/

gaps.subdomain: Modern scholars of ancient free will (Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji, Sharples, Dihle, Long, Salles, Destrée, Fürst)
gaps.name: Pierre Destrée, Ricardo Salles & Marco Zingano (eds.), What is up to us? Studies on Agency and Responsibility in Ancient Philosophy (Academia Verlag, 2014)
gaps.why_canonical: All three editors are named target scholars and a person node 'Destrée / Salles / Zingano (editors)' already exists, implying the volume is referenced — but the volume itself appears absent as a work node. It is the most important recent multi-author collection specifically on to eph' hemin across the ancient tradition and the natural hub linking the Bobzien/Frede/Salles reception layer to the primary eph' hemin concept cluster.
gaps.source: P. Destrée, R. Salles, M. Zingano (eds.), What is up to us? (Academia Verlag 2014)

gaps.subdomain: Modern scholars of ancient free will (Bobzien, Frede, Sorabji, Sharples, Dihle, Long, Salles, Destrée, Fürst)
gaps.name: Anthony Kenny, Aristotle's Theory of the Will (Duckworth, 1979)
gaps.why_canonical: Kenny is present as a person node but his Aristotle's Theory of the Will — the standard counterpoint to Dihle on whether Aristotle possessed a concept of will — is absent. Pairing it with Dihle's claim (Dihle 1982 work node present) that the will is Augustine's invention would complete the 'Discovery of the Will' debate the KG already hosts, anchoring both sides to their defining monographs.
gaps.source: A. Kenny, Aristotle's Theory of the Will (Duckworth 1979); cf. A. Dihle, The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity (UC Press 1982)

gaps.subdomain: Stoics (Zeno→Chrysippus→Posidonius), Epicurus/swerve, Academic skeptics (Carneades), the lazy argument, confatalia
gaps.name: Antipater of Tarsus
gaps.why_canonical: Stoic scholarch (head after Diogenes of Babylon, teacher of Panaetius) who is the named transmitter of the Stoic appeal to divination in the fate debate and is repeatedly cited by Cicero (De Divinatione, De Fato) as defending the Chrysippean line on prediction and the modal status of the future. Bobzien (Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy, 1998) treats Antipater as a distinct voice on the bivalence/divination argument. The KG already has Diogenes of Babylon, Panaetius and Posidonius but the chain skips Antipater entirely, leaving the Zeno→Chrysippus→Posidonius lineage broken at exactly the node where the divination-based determinism argument was reformulated.
gaps.source: Bobzien 1998, Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy; SVF III Antipater; Cicero De Divinatione I.6, De Fato

gaps.subdomain: Stoics (Zeno→Chrysippus→Posidonius), Epicurus/swerve, Academic skeptics (Carneades), the lazy argument, confatalia
gaps.name: Philo the Dialectician (Philo of Megara / Philo Megaricus)
gaps.why_canonical: Megarian/Dialectical-school logician who is the named opponent of Diodorus Cronus on the definition of the possible — the 'Philonian' vs 'Diodorean' modal conceptions are the two poles around which the Master Argument (Kurieuon Logos) and the whole Hellenistic modality-and-fate debate turn. The KG has Diodorus Cronus and the Master Argument reconstructed (Bobzien) but lacks Philo, so the modal contrast that makes the Master Argument intelligible is one-sided. Distinct from the already-present Philo of Larissa and Philo of Alexandria.
gaps.source: Bobzien 1998 ch. on the Master Argument; Sedley, 'Diodorus Cronus and Hellenistic Philosophy' (PCPS 1977); Boethius In De Int. on the Philonian/Diodorean conditional and possible

gaps.subdomain: Stoics (Zeno→Chrysippus→Posidonius), Epicurus/swerve, Academic skeptics (Carneades), the lazy argument, confatalia
gaps.name: Antiochus of Ascalon
gaps.why_canonical: Head of the Academy who broke with Academic skepticism (the 'Old Academy' turn) and is the principal philosophical interlocutor behind Cicero's transmission of both Stoic and Academic positions on fate, assent and the criterion. He is the hinge between Carneades' skeptical legacy (already in the KG) and the Ciceronian sources (De Fato, Academica, both present as works) that preserve the lazy argument and confatalia. His absence leaves the Academic-skeptic-to-Cicero transmission chain undocumented.
gaps.source: Cicero, Academica; J. Barnes & M. Griffin (eds.), 'Philosophia Togata'; SEP entry 'Antiochus of Ascalon'

gaps.subdomain: Stoics (Zeno→Chrysippus→Posidonius), Epicurus/swerve, Academic skeptics (Carneades), the lazy argument, confatalia
gaps.name: Stoic divination-as-proof-of-determinism argument (Chrysippus/Antipater, Cicero De Div. I)
gaps.why_canonical: The positive Stoic argument that the verified existence of divination/prediction proves universal causal determinism (if events can be foreknown, they are fixed in a causal nexus). This is the converse of the lazy argument and one of the two pillars of Chrysippean determinism that Bobzien isolates (alongside bivalence). The KG has Bobzien's note that Chrysippus 'used the existence of divination as proof of causal determinism' but no standalone argument node for it, unlike the lazy argument, master argument, confatalia and cylinder which all have dedicated nodes.
gaps.source: Bobzien 1998, Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy, ch. 2; Cicero De Divinatione I.82-83; De Fato 11-15

gaps.subdomain: Stoics (Zeno→Chrysippus→Posidonius), Epicurus/swerve, Academic skeptics (Carneades), the lazy argument, confatalia
gaps.name: Philonian vs Diodorean modality (definitions of the possible)
gaps.why_canonical: The competing Hellenistic definitions of 'possible': Diodorus' (only what is or will be true is possible) vs Philo's (what is compatible with the internal nature of the thing) vs the Chrysippean refinement. This is the conceptual core of the master-argument/fate dispute and is treated as foundational by every modern reconstruction. The KG has the Sea Battle / future-contingents concept and the Master Argument but no node for the rival modal definitions themselves, which are what the dispute is actually about.
gaps.source: Bobzien 1998 ch. 3-4; Sedley 1977; Boethius, In De Interpretatione editio secunda II.234-235 (Meiser)

gaps.subdomain: Stoics (Zeno→Chrysippus→Posidonius), Epicurus/swerve, Academic skeptics (Carneades), the lazy argument, confatalia
gaps.name: Boethus of Sidon (the Stoic)
gaps.why_canonical: Stoic philosopher (pupil-era of Diogenes of Babylon) who dissented from orthodox Stoic doctrine on conflagration/ekpyrosis and providence, showing the internal diversity of Stoic positions on cosmic determinism. Cited by Diogenes Laertius and Philo (De Aeternitate Mundi). Relevant as a documented intra-Stoic dissent on the very cosmology (ekpyrosis/eternal recurrence — already a concept node) that grounds Stoic fate. Lower priority because his fate-specific testimony is thin.
gaps.source: Diogenes Laertius VII.143, 148; Philo De Aeternitate Mundi 76-78; Algra et al., Cambridge History of Hellenistic Philosophy

gaps.subdomain: Stoics (Zeno→Chrysippus→Posidonius), Epicurus/swerve, Academic skeptics (Carneades), the lazy argument, confatalia
gaps.name: Reaping/recovery (mowing-down) argument and Chrysippus' confatalia reply
gaps.why_canonical: The canonical concrete instantiation of the lazy argument used in the sources ('if it is fated you will recover, you will recover whether or not you call the doctor') and Chrysippus' specific confatalia rebuttal ('calling the doctor is co-fated with recovering'). The KG has the abstract lazy-argument and confatalia nodes plus Origen's and Alexander's versions, but not the dialectical exchange in its classic Ciceronian form (De Fato 28-30) as a structured debate linking the two existing concept nodes.
gaps.source: Cicero De Fato 28-30; Origen Contra Celsum II.20; Bobzien 1998 ch. 5 on the Idle Argument
